Recovered, but not back on track

World life expectancy at birth fell {{dip}} years in the pandemic and was back above its 2019 level by {{back_year}}. In 2023 it stood at {{w2023}} years, still {{trend_gap}} years short of where the trend of 2000–2019 pointed.

1The situation

In 1950 a newborn could expect to live {{w1950}} years at that year’s death rates; in 2023, {{w2023}}. That is a gain of {{gain}} years, {{gain_per_year}} for every calendar year, and the gap between high- and low-income countries shrank from {{inc_gap1950}} to {{inc_gap2023}} years. Two falls break the world line: famine in China around 1960, when life expectancy there dropped from {{china1958}} to {{china1960}}, and the pandemic, which took {{dip}} years between 2019 and {{trough_year}}.

How to read it. Period life expectancy at birth is the average number of years a newborn would live if the death rates of that year held for its whole life. A fall measures that year’s deaths; it is not a forecast for the children born then.

2The trend

By {{back_year}} the world was back above its 2019 level. Against its trend it has not recovered: from 2000 to 2019 life expectancy rose {{trend_decade}} years a decade, and that straight line points to {{trend2023}} years in 2023. The world was {{trend_gap}} years below it, {{band_where}} the line’s 95 % prediction interval (±{{pi2023}}).

What the dotted line is not. It extends the trend of 2000–2019 only to measure the gap. It is not a forecast: nothing in the data says that life expectancy will rejoin the line, or keep rising at that pace.

{{trend_gap}} years

separate the world in 2023 from the line it followed for twenty years. A return to 2019 is not a return to the trend.

3The gap

Where a child is born matters more than the pandemic did. In 2023 life expectancy ranged from {{map_min}} years in {{map_min_name}} to {{map_max}} in {{map_max_name}} across the {{map_n}} countries on the map. The gap between high- and low-income countries, {{inc_gap2023}} years, is {{gap_over_dip}} times the world’s pandemic fall.

Reading the map. Each class holds a fifth of the countries. Small countries vanish at this scale; Figure 4 gives the {{pop_n}} most populous, {{pop_share}} % of all people.

Sources and method

Data. Period life expectancy at birth: UN World Population Prospects (2024), Human Mortality Database (2024), Zijdeman and Ribeira da Silva (2015), Riley (2005); processed by Our World in Data, downloaded 2026‑10‑12, CC BY 4.0. Outlines and population estimates for 2019: Natural Earth v5.1.2, public domain.

Method. The pandemic fall is the value of 2019 less the lowest of 2020–2022. The trend is a least-squares line through the world values of 2000–2019 ({{slope}} years a year) with its 95 % prediction interval. The map is in the Equal Earth projection (Šavrič, Patterson and Jenny 2018), without Antarctica.

Reproduce. python examples/python/report/make_report.py recomputes every number from the two data files, redraws the figures and prints these pages.

4The options

The figures suggest three options. They are examples of the layout, not recommendations.

Measure against the trend

A return to the 2019 level ({{above2019_signed}} years by 2023) reads as recovery. Against the trend of 2000–2019 the world is {{trend_gap}} years short. Reporting both keeps the distance in sight.

Look where the fall was deepest

From 2019 to the lowest pandemic year, lower-middle-income countries lost {{lmi_dip}} years, upper-middle-income {{umi_dip}}, high-income {{high_dip}} and low-income {{low_dip}}.

Keep the long gap in view

High-income countries live {{inc_gap2023}} years longer than low-income ones, down from {{inc_gap1950}} in 1950: {{gap_over_dip}} times the world’s pandemic fall of {{dip}} years.

5The ask

An example of an ask. Publish world and income-group life expectancy every year beside the trend of 2000–2019, with the distance to it, until the {{trend_gap}}-year gap closes.

This shows how the layout states an ask. It is an illustration, not advice to any organisation.
